standard.title: Government economic intervention
standard.description: the ways that government intervenes in the economy to improve economic performance and living standards within Australian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how economic decision-making involves the interdependence of consumers, businesses, the financial sector and government (AC9HE9K02). They have explored how Australia trades with other nations and its patterns with Asia (AC9HE9K03). They can explain how different actors in the economy interact and how decisions ripple across the system. Students have also begun working with AC9HE10K01 — how economic indicators signal the need for government response.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the ways that the Australian Government intervenes in the economy through fiscal policy, income redistribution and regulation to improve economic performance and living standards.

nodes.label: What government intervention means
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why markets alone do not always produce desirable outcomes and why governments intervene in the economy.
nodes.minimum_width: State at least two reasons why the Australian Government intervenes in the economy (e.g. to address market failure, improve living standards, reduce inequality).
nodes.typical_width: Explain the rationale for government intervention — market failure, inequality, unemployment and poverty — and identify the general categories of government tools available (fiscal policy, income redistribution, regulation).
wider: Examine a specific market failure (e.g. pollution, public goods provision, monopoly) and evaluate why the market alone cannot address it
Compare the case for and against government intervention using a contemporary Australian policy debate (e.g. housing affordability, energy markets)
Investigate how views on the appropriate scope of government intervention have changed over time in Australia
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand that intervention is a response to a problem — not an arbitrary action — will describe policies without explaining their purpose. The rationale is the connective tissue linking indicator signals (K01) to specific policy tools.

response_modes.reason: Build the logic chain: what the market produces without intervention → what problem this creates → what the government can do about it. This scaffold prevents students from treating policies as a list to memorise rather than responses to economic conditions.

success_criteria: States at least two reasons why governments intervene in the economy
Connects a reason for intervention to a category of government tool (e.g. inequality → redistribution)

nodes.label: Fiscal policy and the federal Budget
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how the Australian Government uses fiscal policy — taxation and expenditure — to influence economic performance and living standards.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what fiscal policy is and give one example each of how the government uses taxation and expenditure to influence the economy.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how the Australian Government uses fiscal policy to improve standard of living — including the federal Budget, taxation settings and expenditure on skills training and workforce development; distinguish between expansionary and contractionary fiscal stances.
wider: Analyse a specific federal Budget measure (e.g. infrastructure investment, skills package) and evaluate its expected impact on economic performance and who benefits
Compare the fiscal policy responses of Australia and another country to a shared economic shock and explain differences in approach
Investigate how automatic stabilisers (e.g. unemployment benefits) function as fiscal policy without requiring Budget decisions
nodes.hinge_reason: Fiscal policy is the primary instrument the descriptor names. Students who cannot explain the taxation-expenditure mechanism cannot meet the descriptor's scope — all downstream analysis of income redistribution and welfare depends on understanding how the Budget works.

response_modes.reason: Use multiple real Budget examples — infrastructure, social services, tax cuts — so students can apply the fiscal policy concept across varied contexts rather than memorising one example.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Federal Budget analysis is rich and annually renewable content. Students who can analyse specific measures across different budget years develop genuine evaluative capacity around fiscal choices.
success_criteria: Explains what fiscal policy is and distinguishes taxation from expenditure as tools
Gives a specific example of how a Budget measure is intended to influence an economic outcome

nodes.label: Income redistribution and living standards
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how and why the government redistributes income, and identify the mechanisms through which redistribution affects living standards and inequality.
nodes.minimum_width: Name one type of income transfer (e.g. pension, youth allowance) and one universal service (e.g. healthcare, education) and explain how each affects living standards.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how the government redistributes income to achieve a more equal distribution — including income transfers (pensions, youth allowance, job search) and provision of universal services (healthcare, education); explain the forces that create variation in living standards (unemployment, poverty) and why redistribution is a policy response.
wider: Investigate how Australia's Gini coefficient has changed over time and evaluate whether government redistribution has been effective in reducing inequality
Compare the scope and design of Australia's income support system with that of another country (e.g. Nordic model vs US model) and examine trade-offs
Examine how specific communities (e.g. First Nations Australians, regional communities) experience living standards variation and what targeted government responses exist

response_modes.reason: Variety of redistribution mechanisms prevents students from treating this as a single category. Differentiating income transfers from universal service provision clarifies the mechanism and enables more precise explanation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations living standards variation, international comparisons, and inequality data offer genuinely rich directions — not just more examples of the same type. Students who engage with these develop evaluative capacity about equity and policy effectiveness.
success_criteria: Distinguishes income transfers from universal service provision as redistribution mechanisms
Explains how at least one redistribution mechanism affects living standards for a specific group

nodes.label: The Reserve Bank and monetary policy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the role and function of the Reserve Bank of Australia and explain how monetary policy tools (particularly the cash rate) are used to manage economic performance.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the Reserve Bank of Australia's primary role and explain one way it influences the economy (e.g. through the cash rate).
nodes.typical_width: Explain the role and function of the RBA within the Australian economy — including its independence, inflation target mandate and use of the cash rate to influence borrowing costs, consumer spending and investment.
wider: Trace the transmission mechanism from RBA cash rate decision to household mortgage repayments to consumer spending to economic growth
Compare a period of rate rises (e.g. 2022–2023) with a period of rate cuts (e.g. 2020) and explain the RBA's stated reasoning in each case
Evaluate the limits of monetary policy — situations where interest rate adjustment does not produce expected economic outcomes

response_modes.reason: The transmission mechanism from RBA decision to economic outcomes involves multiple steps and can be confusing without explicit scaffolding. Map the chain clearly: RBA decision → bank interest rates → borrowing behaviour → spending → economic activity.

success_criteria: States the RBA's primary mandate and one tool it uses
Explains how a change in the cash rate influences economic behaviour (even if the chain is simplified)

nodes.label: Government intervention — integrated evaluation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain multiple ways the Australian Government intervenes in the economy and evaluate how these tools together aim to improve economic performance and living standards.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain two distinct ways the government intervenes (e.g. fiscal policy and income redistribution) and describe what each is trying to achieve.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how fiscal policy, income redistribution and monetary policy work together as a suite of government interventions aimed at improving economic performance and living standards; discuss variation in living standards and how government tools address it.
wider: Evaluate a current or recent government economic policy package, identifying which intervention types are present and assessing whether the mix is coherent
Investigate how the government's economic intervention approach has shifted under different political administrations and what this reveals about assumptions behind the tools
Examine how intervention affects different groups unequally — who benefits most from fiscal expansion, who bears the burden of monetary tightening

response_modes.reason: This node draws fiscal policy, redistribution and monetary policy together into a coherent picture of government economic management. The integration demand is the descriptor's full scope — explaining the *ways* (plural) of intervention.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two distinct types of government intervention and explains what each aims to achieve
Explains how both tools relate to improving economic performance or living standards
